common_name: Jetstream Oakleaf Hydrangea (Compact Upright Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Jetstream stays more compact and upright than older, larger oakleaf hydrangea cultivars like Alice, fitting smaller foundation and border plantings.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Jetstream bears large, upright, cone-shaped white flower panicles that age to a soft pink over a more compact, tidy, upright shrub than older oakleaf hydrangea selections, fitting smaller foundation beds and mixed borders without sacrificing the bold, deeply lobed foliage and outstanding orange-red-purple fall color the species is known for. Its exfoliating, cinnamon-colored bark adds winter interest after leaves drop. As with other oakleaf hydrangeas, flower buds form on the previous year's wood, so prune only in the weeks immediately following bloom to avoid removing next year's flowers.

common_name: Queen of Hearts Oakleaf Hydrangea (Deep Pink-Red Panicle Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Queen of Hearts was bred for flower panicles that deepen to an unusually strong pink-red as they age.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Queen of Hearts, developed at North Carolina State University, bears large, upright flower panicles that open white and mature to an unusually deep, saturated pink-red, a richer color than most oakleaf hydrangea cultivars achieve, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with bold, deeply lobed leaves that turn brilliant orange-red-purple in fall. Its strong flower color and vigor have made it a standout in university breeding trials. As with other oakleaf hydrangeas, flower buds form on old wood, so prune only in the weeks immediately following bloom to avoid sacrificing the next season's flowers. Its exfoliating, cinnamon-colored bark adds structure through winter after leaves drop.

common_name: Invincibelle Ruby Hydrangea (Deep Pink-Red Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Invincibelle Ruby bears some of the deepest, most saturated pink-red flower color in the Invincibelle smooth hydrangea series.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Invincibelle Ruby produces rounded flower heads that open a deep pink and mature to an unusually rich ruby-red, one of the darkest colors in the reblooming Invincibelle series of native smooth hydrangeas, on strong stems that hold the flower heads upright without flopping. It blooms on new growth from summer into fall, so unlike oakleaf and bigleaf hydrangeas, it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and deadheading spent blooms encourages continued rebloom. This native species tolerates more sun and a wider range of soil conditions than bigleaf hydrangea, making it a reliable choice for borders and foundation plantings across a broad range of climates.

common_name: Incrediball Blush Hydrangea (Giant Pink-Blushed White Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Incrediball Blush bears the same enormous flower heads as Incrediball but blushed with soft pink.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Incrediball Blush produces enormous, basketball-sized rounded flower heads on the same extra-sturdy, non-flopping stems that made the original Incrediball famous, but with a soft, romantic pink blush overlaying the white florets that deepens slightly as flowers age. It blooms on new growth from summer into fall, so it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, unlike oakleaf and bigleaf hydrangeas. This native species tolerates more sun and a wider range of soil conditions than bigleaf hydrangea, and its massive flower heads make a bold statement as a specimen or informal hedge in a mixed border.

common_name: Invincibelle Mini Mauvette Hydrangea (Dwarf Mauve-Pink Reblooming Smooth Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Invincibelle Mini Mauvette is a dwarf selection within the reblooming Invincibelle series, fitting small borders and containers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun. Invincibelle Mini Mauvette produces rounded flower heads in a soft mauve-pink on a notably dwarf, dense plant, the smallest in the reblooming Invincibelle series of native smooth hydrangeas, making it well suited to small borders, foundation plantings, and large containers where full-size smooth hydrangeas would be too large. It blooms on new growth from summer into fall, so it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers, and deadheading spent blooms encourages continued rebloom. This native species tolerates more sun and a wider range of soil conditions than bigleaf hydrangea, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for small-space gardens.
